In summary, our research is concerned with
two main aspects of STS systems: (i) the interpretability of the system output, and (ii) how to use this interpretability to produce explanations in natural languages that can be used by humans.

the following contributions: 1) we introduce a formalization for iSTS, which is a graded and typed alignment between two sentences; 2) we present a dataset of sentence pairs, annotated following the formalized task; 3) we develop an iSTS model trained on the dataset, showing that our formalization and the dataset are feasible; and 4) we show how the iSTA model output can be used as an explanation for users.

we present the first dataset and method for producing explanations of STS systems, which are useful to help users understand their output.

we have proposed a formalism for interpretability in STS and have built a dataset and a system that can be used to generate graded typed segment alignment between two sentences, as well as to generate explanations in natural language, which can help users understand the STS systems output.
we present a new dataset, a new task, and a new method for producing natural language explanations for STS systems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we propose a novel formalization for the task of interpretability of semantic textual similarity and provide a dataset and an automatic system that can be used for this task.
we propose a new dataset for the Semantic Textual Similairty task that can be used to develop interpretable systems.

we formalize interpretability for the STS task; we build a publicly available iSTS dataset; we develop an iSTS baseline system; we show that the iSTS output can be used for automatic explanation generation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to add an interpretablity layer to a STS system that helps humans better understand the reasoning behind the system's decisions.

the interpretability layer can be seen as a new dimension of the problem of semantic textual similarity, where we can measure not only how similar two sentences are, but also what they have in common and where they differ.
it is possible to develop systems that can automatically produce explanations, which are useful to humans.
